p58: 58.  According to the Court’s settled case-law, the expression “in accordance with the law” not only requires that the impugned measure should have a basis in domestic law, but also refers to the quality of the law in question, requiring that it should be accessible to the person concerned and foreseeable as to its effects (see, among many other authorities, Amann v. Switzerland [GC], no. 27798/95, § 50, ECHR 2000-II; Slivenko v. Latvia [GC], no. 48321/99, § 100, ECHR 2003-X; and Kurić and Others v. Slovenia [GC], no. 26828/06, § 341, ECHR 2012).
p59: 59.  The Court observes that the decision ordering the child’s return to Australia was taken by the Rīga Regional Court on the basis of the Hague Convention, an instrument signed and ratified by Latvia in 1982. Furthermore, the Latvian Civil Procedure Law, Article 644 of which governs matters relating to the wrongful removal of children to Latvia, makes its application subject to the express condition of compliance with the Hague Convention, the “Brussels II bis Regulation” and the European Convention on Human Rights.
p60: 60.  The applicant submitted that at the time of her departure from Australia she had been exercising sole parental responsibility for her daughter.
p61: 61.  The Court notes, however, that this issue was expressly examined by the Latvian courts dealing with the request for return. Those courts applied, while stating that they could neither interpret nor amend it, the decision of the Australian Family Court of 6 November 2008, which had confirmed T.’s paternity and the existence of joint parental responsibility for the child since her birth. Consequently, both the District Court and the Rīga Regional Court held that T.’s request was in conformity with the Hague Convention in that respect.
p62: 62.  Furthermore, the Court considers that it is not its task to determine whether or not an international removal of a child was “wrongful” within the meaning of Article 3 of the Hague Convention. It is not its function to deal with errors of fact or law allegedly committed by a national court unless and in so far as they may have infringed rights and freedoms protected by the Convention (see García Ruiz v. Spain [GC], no. 30544/96, § 28, ECHR 1999-I): it is for the national courts to resolve problems of interpretation and application of domestic legislation, and of rules of general international law and international treaties (see Maumousseau and Washington v. France, no. 39388/05, § 79, 6 December 2007, and Neulinger and Shuruk, cited above, § 100). In the present case the applicant, besides having failed to make use of the available remedies to challenge the Australian decision confirming T.’s paternity and the existence of joint parental responsibility for the child at the time of her departure from Australia – an issue which relates directly to the preconditions for the application of the Hague Convention –, has shown neither that it was impossible for her to challenge the Australian decision nor in what way the domestic courts failed in that regard.
p63: 63.  In conclusion, the Court considers that the interference in issue was in accordance with the law within the meaning of Article 8 of the Convention.
p64: 64.  The Chamber found that the interference had pursued the aim of protecting the rights of T. and the child, which was a legitimate aim within the meaning of Article 8 § 2 of the Convention.
p65: 65.  The applicant did not comment on this point.
p66: 66.  According to the Government, the interference pursued a legitimate aim, namely the protection of the rights and freedoms of T. and his daughter.
p67: 67.  The Grand Chamber shares the Chamber’s view that the return order pursued the legitimate aim of protecting the rights and freedoms of T. and E., which, moreover, was not disputed by the parties before it.
